newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Inflation is bright spot in murky Russia economy.
newsitem.headline: Inflation is bright spot in murky Russia economy.

text.p: Russian inflation slid to new year-on-year lows in September, but wage arrears rose steeply and industrial production shrank in an economy struggling to rake in taxes and pay workers on time.

The State Statistics Committee said consumer prices rose just 31.7 percent in the year to September, the lowest level since economic reforms got under way in January 1992 and down from 37.1 percent in August.
But September industrial production was 6.8 percent lower than a year earlier, dashing economists' hopes that a prolonged economic slump was about to come to an end.
Wage arrears rose 10 percent in September alone, hitting a total of over 40 trillion roubles ($9 billion). Arrears were 36 trillion roubles in August.

Wage and tax arrears are two of the biggest problems facing the Russian economy and officials announced new plans to tackle the tax problem on Tuesday, threatening to sue six firms for bankruptcy unless they paid their tax bills within a week.
"We cannot allow our most profitable companies to break the laws of God and society," Pyotr Mostovoi, head of the state bankruptcy agency, told a news conference.
"The debts make fractions of a percent of these companies' turnovers and none of them can say it is incapable of paying."
President Boris Yeltsin last week announced the creation of an emergency commission to work out how to resolve the tax problem and bring in extra cash.

"I know taxes are high in Russia today, but we will be able to lower them only if we manage to ensure compliance with tax legislation," said Yeltsin, who faces an operation in the next two months to improve the blood supply to his heart.
"First we collect taxes and then we will cut them," he said.
But many economists have cast doubt on the government's ability to enforce plans to raise extra cash.

Domestic financial markets are more interested in Yeltsin's health than in the tax problem and Russian shares eased on Tuesday after a Russian radio station said the president was too ill to undergo a planned heart operation.
The Kremlin denied the rumours and said preparations for the operations were running on schedule.
"Although the rumours were dispelled, maybe someone decided to take profits and prices slipped," said Andrei Ippolitov, corporate securities director at IK Prospekt.

The International Monetary Fund, which has blessed Russian economic reforms with a $10 billion three-year loan, is watching tax collection carefully as a pointer to Russia's ability to meet its budget targets.
A new team of IMF experts arrives in Moscow on Wednesday to assess the latest figures. The fund delayed paying a tranche of the loan this summer because it was worried about tax revenues.
The State Duma lower house of parliament, dominated by communists and their nationalist allies, is also examining the government's budget plans carefully.
The Duma rejected the draft 1997 budget on Friday and has asked the government to come up with new proposals within 10 days.
Many deputies say the proposals do not offer enough protection to those who lost out under economic reforms and others say spending must be increased to help ailing firms.
